newsitem.title: USA: Dlr closes near new highs, strikes 127 yen in U.S.
newsitem.headline: Dlr closes near new highs, strikes 127 yen in U.S.

text.p: The dollar closed stronger after reaching a 37-month high against the mark and a more than four-and-a-half year peak at 127 yen, as concerns about central bank intervention faded, dealers said.
The strength of the U.S. economy and its relatively high interest rates also continued to bolster the greenback.

"It's nothing new ... just a general belief that central banks are not going to be concerned about a move higher, so in the market's mind they've gotten the green light to take it higher," said Richard Vullo, a vice president at Bayerische Hypothenken und Weschelsbank.

The dollar reached its highest since August 1992 against the yen in New York trading, stretching a gain posted Wednesday in Asia after U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin denied suggestions he had discussed curbing the dollar's rise with senior Japanese officials in Tokyo last week.
Dollar/mark also topped its March high at 1.7210. Stop-loss buying and investors looking to get long dollars catapulted it to 1.7270, its highest since February 1994.
"They had targets of the old highs ... I think it was just some of the bigger players gunning for those levels," Vullo said.
The dollar ended at 126.85/90 yen, up from 126.48/53 at the open and at 1.7258/63 marks, up from 1.7175/78 marks.

Wariness of central banks has slowed the dollar's rise since February when finance officials from the Group of Seven industrial nations stated the dollar's rally from record lows in 1995 had corrected major misalignments in exchange rates.
Japanese officials in particular have seemed to want to stem the dollar's rise, worried that the weak yen might do additional damage to their fragile financial markets.

In overseas trade, the dollar shrugged off remarks by Eisuke Sakakibara, the director-general of the Japanese Finance Ministry's International Finance Bureau, who said intervention in the currency markets by Japan was possible if exchange rates get substantially out of line with relative economic conditions in Japan and the U.S.

But after the quarter-point interest rate increase by the Federal Reserve on March 25, investors comparing the stumbling economies of Japan and Europe to robust U.S. growth viewed the economic fundamentals as highly favorable for the dollar at the moment, traders said.

"There is very little advantage to hold marks. I mean its a very expensive proposition right now, based on interest rates and the prospects for just general growth in Europe versus America," said Diego Giurleo, a vice president at Royal Bank of Canada in New York.
"If you look at the yen, there is the other issue, which is the weakness of the (Japanese) financial system, which more or less precludes any tightening in monetary policy there," Giurleo added.
Elsewhere, the dollar rose to 1.4795/05 Swiss francs at the close from 1.4735/40 Swiss and to Canadian $1.3891/96 from C$1.3844/49. The pound fell to $1.6185/95 from $1.6228/38.
The Australian dollar climbed to $0.7844/49 from $0.7820/25.
